title: Psalm 91: In the Shadow of the Almighty
summary: The psalm describes the security of the one who dwells in the shelter of the Most High: God delivers him from the fowler's snare and the deadly plague, covers him with his wings, and commands his angels to guard him. Terrors by night and arrows by day will not overcome him, though thousands fall around him. In the closing lines God himself speaks, promising to deliver, answer, honor, and satisfy the one who loves him and knows his name.
story: Psalm 91 follows Psalm 90's sober meditation on human frailty and God's wrath, and it answers that psalm's closing plea. Psalm 90 called God "our dwelling place"; Psalm 91 describes the one who "has made the LORD your dwelling" (verse 9, using the same Hebrew word). Where Psalm 90 ended by asking God to satisfy his people with his love, Psalm 91 ends with God's promise to satisfy the faithful with long life and to show them his salvation. In Book IV, which responds to the loss of the Davidic throne by proclaiming God's kingship, this psalm offers personal assurance: whatever has happened to Israel's kings, those who take refuge in God are held in his care. It leads into Psalm 92's song of thanks and the proclamations that the LORD reigns.
historical:
Psalm 91 has no heading in the Hebrew text, one of a number of untitled psalms in Book IV. The ancient Greek translation, the Septuagint, gives it a heading attributing it to David. Some ancient Jewish interpreters, following a principle that an untitled psalm belongs to the author of the one before it, connected it with Moses, since Psalm 90 bears his name. Modern scholars generally see it as a temple psalm of uncertain date, and some suggest it was spoken by a priest to a worshiper seeking refuge in the sanctuary, with verses 14 to 16 as a divine oracle pronounced over him.

The psalm was prized in antiquity as a prayer for protection against evil. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, found at Qumran and dating from about the last two centuries BC to the first century AD, a scroll containing songs against evil spirits includes a form of this psalm. Later Jewish and Christian communities also used it as a prayer at night and in times of danger, and it has long been prayed in times of plague.
cultural:
The dangers the psalm names were everyday threats in the ancient world. The fowler set snares and nets to catch birds, and the image stood for hidden traps laid by enemies. Plague and pestilence swept through cities and armies with no known cause or cure; many ancient peoples attributed them to demons or angry gods. Terrors of the night, arrows by day, disease stalking in darkness, and destruction at noon cover every hour, and some interpreters think the psalm alludes to popular beliefs about spirits associated with certain times of day. Lions and cobras were real dangers in the land and in the wilderness.

The image of God covering his people with feathers and wings draws on the picture of a mother bird sheltering her young (compare Deuteronomy 32:11). Some interpreters also connect it with the wings of the cherubim over the ark of the covenant in the temple's inner sanctuary, where God was enthroned, so that sheltering under his wings meant finding refuge in his presence at the temple (compare Psalms 36:7 and 61:4). Shield and rampart were the defenses of a soldier and a city.
literary: Psalm 91 is a psalm of trust with strong wisdom elements. Its most distinctive feature is its change of speakers. Verse 1 states a general truth about the one who dwells with the Most High. In verse 2 a voice answers in the first person: "I will say to the LORD, ‘You are my refuge and my fortress’". Verses 3 to 13 then address a "you", often understood as a priest or teacher speaking to a worshiper, piling up assurances. Verses 14 to 16 shift again to God's own voice, speaking of the faithful one in the third person with a string of promises: I will deliver, protect, answer, be with, deliver, honor, satisfy, and show. The psalm uses four names for God in its first two verses (Most High, Almighty, LORD, and God), gathering his titles around the one who trusts him. Pairs of opposites, night and day, darkness and noon, a thousand and ten thousand, stress that there is no time or place outside God's protection.

outline.t: Dwelling in the shelter of the Most High
Protection from snare, plague, terror, and arrow
Angels to guard you in all your ways
God's promise to the one who loves him

doctrines.note: The psalm confesses that God's care covers every danger and every hour, and that he commands his angels to guard his people. Nothing that threatens them is outside his authority.
The promises belong to the one who dwells in God's shelter, makes the LORD his refuge, loves him, and knows his name. The psalm describes trust as a place one lives, not a single act.
The psalm ends with God's promise: "show him My salvation". Salvation is deliverance from danger and, more deeply, the experience of God's presence and faithfulness.

words.note: Shaddai, Almighty. An ancient name for God associated with the patriarchs (Exodus 6:3 says God appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty). Its origin is debated; suggestions include a connection with mountains or with the idea of power. Here it stands alongside Most High to name the God whose shadow is a shelter.

Kanaph, wing. The word can mean a bird's wing or the edge of a garment. God's wings are an image of tender protection. Ruth seeks refuge under the wings of the God of Israel (Ruth 2:12), and Boaz is asked to spread his garment's wing over her (Ruth 3:9).

Malak, messenger or angel. The same word describes human messengers and heavenly ones. In verse 11 God commands his angels to guard the faithful, one of the Old Testament passages that shaped the belief that God assigns angels to protect his people.

christ: Psalm 91 is quoted in the Gospels by the devil. During Jesus' temptation in the wilderness, Satan takes him to the pinnacle of the temple and cites verses 11 and 12, urging him to throw himself down so that angels will catch him (Matthew 4:6; Luke 4:10-11). Jesus refuses, answering with Deuteronomy 6:16, which forbids putting God to the test. The scene shows how the psalm is rightly read: its promises are for those who trust God, not for those who try to force his hand. Jesus is the one who most fully dwelt in the shelter of the Most High, and his trust led him not away from suffering but through it. God did not keep him from the cross, but he did deliver and honor him and show him salvation by raising him from the dead, which is the fullest keeping of the promise in verses 14 to 16. The psalm also anticipates Jesus' authority over evil, and he tells his disciples that he has given them authority to tread on serpents and scorpions (Luke 10:19).

hard.q: Faithful people do die of plague and fall in battle. How can this psalm promise that no harm will come near?
hard.a:
Taken as a guarantee that believers will never suffer, the psalm would be contradicted by much of Scripture and by ordinary experience. Job suffered, prophets were killed, and Jesus himself was crucified. Readers have taken several approaches. Many interpreters read the psalm as poetry of trust, describing the fundamental security of those whose lives are in God's hands rather than promising exemption from every physical danger. It speaks, on this view, the way a parent's reassurance speaks: true at its root, not an insurance policy.

Others read the psalm in light of its ending: God promises to be with the faithful one in trouble (verse 15), which assumes trouble will come. Its deepest promise is God's presence and final deliverance. Still others note that the Old Testament often speaks in general terms of how God's world works, as Proverbs does, without claiming there are no exceptions. The temptation of Jesus adds a warning: the devil used these very verses to encourage presumption. The psalm invites trust, not testing.

questions: The psalm describes dwelling, not visiting, in the shelter of the Most High. What would it look like for your trust in God to be a place you live?
Satan quoted this psalm to Jesus. How can Scripture be misused, and how does Jesus' response help you read promises like these well?
Verse 15 says, "I will be with him in trouble." How does that promise change the way you think about the rest of the psalm's assurances?
